citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on a measurable observation space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$; IID means a common law and mutual independence of the whole family ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). Let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $m_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and assume $P|m_\theta|<\infty$. Define
$$P_nm_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n m_\theta(X_i),\qquad Pm_\theta=\int m_\theta\,dP.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is an **M-estimator** if it maximizes or minimizes $\theta\mapsto P_nm_\theta$; measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]. It is an exact maximizer when $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$, and an $o_P(1)$-approximate maximizer when the finite measurable gap $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta-P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}$ is $o_P(1)$. For minimization use the gap $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$. The notation $o_P(1)$ is that of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

The maximizing and minimizing forms are both included; replacing $m_\theta$ by $-m_\theta$ converts one to the other. This definition does not assert that a maximizer exists, nor that the population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has a unique maximizer. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into the empirical or population criterion, assume that evaluation is measurable and finite.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

derivations.claim: Put $\Delta_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|$ and $r_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}$. By assumption $\Delta_n\to_P0$ and $r_n\to_P0$. Since $\hat\theta_n$ is an approximate maximizer by [F8], $P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\ge P_n\ell_{\theta^*}-r_n$, and therefore $0\le M(\theta^*)-M(\hat\theta_n)\le2\Delta_n+r_n$.

For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, separation gives a positive gap $\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\|\hat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Step 1.1 then gives $P(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon)\le P(2\Delta_n+r_n\ge\eta_\varepsilon)\to0$. Thus $\hat\theta_n-\theta^*=o_P(1)$ by [F6], so with probability tending to one the segment from $\theta^*$ to $\hat\theta_n$ lies in any fixed neighborhood on which the score is differentiable.

Choose a ball about $\theta^*$ inside the differentiability neighborhood; the measurable event that $\hat\theta_n$ lies in this ball ensures its segment from $\theta^*$ stays in that neighborhood. On this event define $A_n=\int_0^1 P_n\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*+t(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)}\,dt$; set $A_n=H$ otherwise. For each fixed parameter in a smaller ball, density measurability makes the log-density measurable, and difference quotients make the sections of $S_\theta$ and $\nabla_\theta S_\theta$ measurable. On compact subballs, rounding parameters to rational grids gives countable-valued Borel approximations; continuity in $\theta$ makes the score and Hessian fields jointly measurable as pointwise limits. The segment integrand is then measurable, and its continuous sample paths make $A_n$ the limit of measurable Riemann sums. Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $D$ at $\theta^*$ supplies a sufficiently small fixed $\delta$ for which $\|D(\theta)-H\|_{op}<\varepsilon/2$ throughout the $\delta$-ball. Consistency from step 2.1 and the assumed uniform Hessian law imply $P(\|A_n-H\|_{op}>\varepsilon)\to0$.

On the same high-probability event, the componentwise fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment gives $P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=P_nS_{\theta^*}+A_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)$. By step 3.1, every entry of $A_n-H$ tends to zero in probability. The determinant and adjugate are polynomials in the entries, so $\det A_n\to_P\det H\ne0$ and $\operatorname{adj}(A_n)\to_P\operatorname{adj}(H)$; on the event $\det A_n\ne0$, $A_n^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A_n)/\det A_n$, hence every entry of $A_n^{-1}-H^{-1}$ tends to zero in probability. The finite-dimensional matrix bound $\|B\|_{op}\le d\max_{j,k}|B_{jk}|$ then gives $\|A_n^{-1}-H^{-1}\|_{op}\to_P0$. Rearranging gives $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)=-A_n^{-1}\sqrt nP_nS_{\theta^*}+A_n^{-1}\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}$ on an event whose probability tends to one.

By [F2], the score vectors $S_{\theta^*}(X_i)$ are IID; their mean is zero and their covariance is $J$. Their second moment is finite by the Statement, so [F4] and [A1] give $\sqrt nP_nS_{\theta^*}\Rightarrow G$ with $G\sim N_d(0,J)$. The matrix $A_n^{-1}$ converges in probability in operator norm to $H^{-1}$, and the residual vector $\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$ by the Statement. Flattening the matrix entries and concatenating the vectors gives a finite-dimensional vector converging in probability to $(H^{-1},0)$. Applying [F5] to the continuous map $(x,A,r)\mapsto-Ax+Ar$ gives the limit $-H^{-1}G$. Its covariance is $H^{-1}JH^{-T}$, proving the assertion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

derivations.claim: On the unit sphere $S^{d-1}$ of [F2], the function $u\mapsto u^TIu$ is continuous and strictly positive. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

This is the distance from $x$ to $C$ in the norm induced by $I$. The definition uses an infimum; attainment is proved separately when a later result requires it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of

Let $d\ge1$, let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric matrix such that $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^d$, let $z\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and closed in the Euclidean metric. Define $q_z(h):=z^Th-\tfrac12h^TIh$. Then there is a constant $\lambda>0$ such that $h^TIh\ge\lambda\|h\|_2^2$ for all $h$, $q_z$ attains its maximum on $C$, and

$$\sup_{h\in C}q_z(h)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C).$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

The lower bound in [F6] and [F5] imply $\|h_A(z)\|_2\le2\|z\|_2/\lambda$ (with the bound immediate when $h_A(z)=0$).

Let $\lambda$ be from [F6], fix $M>0$, and choose $R>2M/\lambda+1$. For $A_n=C_n$, $A=C$ (and likewise for $A_n=C_{0n}$, $A=C_0$), write $m_{A_n,R}(z)=\sup_{h\in A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)}q_z(h)$. points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

derivations.claim: On the probability-one event $0<X_{(n)}\le\theta$, the likelihood at a candidate $u>0$ is $L_n(u)=\prod_{i=1}^np_u(X_i)=u^{-n}\mathbf1\{X_{(n)}\le u\}$. It is zero for $u<X_{(n)}$, while for $u\ge X_{(n)}$ it equals $u^{-n}\le X_{(n)}^{-n}=L_n(X_{(n)})$, with strict inequality if $u>X_{(n)}$. Thus $X_{(n)}$ maximizes the likelihood almost surely; on the null event $X_{(n)}=0$, use the arbitrary positive assignment specified above.

For $0\le t<n\theta$, independence and the uniform CDF give $P_\theta\{n(\theta-X_{(n)})>t\}=P_\theta\{X_i<\theta-t/n\text{ for every }i\}=(1-t/(n\theta))^n$. For fixed $t\ge0$ this formula applies for all sufficiently large $n$, and its limit is $e^{-t/\theta}$.

For every $h>0$ small enough that $\theta+h>0$, the gained support interval $(\theta,\theta+h]$ has $p_\theta=0$ and $p_{\theta+h}=1/(\theta+h)$. If the model were QMD at $\theta$, the score term in [F2] would vanish on this interval and the squared remainder integral would be at least $\int_\theta^{\theta+h}p_{\theta+h}(x)\,dx=h/(\theta+h)$. But $[h/(\theta+h)]/h^2=1/[h(\theta+h)]\to\infty$, contradicting the required $o(h^2)$ remainder. Thus the model is not QMD at $\theta$.

derivations.claim: Therefore the nonnegative variable $n(\theta-X_{(n)})$ converges in distribution to the exponential law with rate $1/\theta$, whose CDF is $0$ for $t<0$ and $1-e^{-t/\theta}$ for $t\ge0$. The limiting CDF is continuous, so [F3] applies at every real $t$.

For any $\varepsilon>0$ and all $n>\varepsilon^2/\theta^2$, the exact maximum formula gives $P_\theta\{\sqrt n(\theta-X_{(n)})>\varepsilon\}=(1-\varepsilon/(\theta\sqrt n))^n\to0$. Thus $\sqrt n(\theta-X_{(n)})\to_P0$ by [F4], refuting the stated nonzero root-$n$ fluctuation and confirming the faster $n$ rate in step 2.1.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

On the null event $X_{(n)}=0$, the likelihood is $\vartheta^{-n}$ and is unbounded as $\vartheta\downarrow0$, so no maximizer exists there; a fixed positive fallback is only a measurable extension, not an MLE on that event. Applying [F2] identifies the exact rate and limit law.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$. Assume the full-model parameter set $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$, so $\theta_0$ is interior for the QMD model. Under $P_{\theta_0}$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i)$ be their sample log-likelihood. Define local parameter sets $C_n:=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ and $C_{0n}:=\sqrt n(\Theta_0-\theta_0)$. Assume the model is QMD at $\theta_0$ as in [[def-qmd-path]], and write $I:=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ for its Fisher information; assume $I$ is positive definite, meaning $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Suppose $C_n$ and $C_{0n}$ are closed in the Euclidean metric (their complements are open), contain $0$, and converge locally to nonempty closed convex cones $C$ and $C_0$ with $C_0\subseteq C$. A cone contains $0$ and is closed under multiplication by every nonnegative scalar; convex means that the set contains the line segment between each pair of its points. Local convergence means that, for every $R>0$, there are $\delta_{n,R}\to0$ such that every point of $C_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ or $C\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}$ in Euclidean distance of the other set, and likewise for $C_{0n}$ and $C_0$. Here a point $x$ is within $\delta$ of a set $A$ when $\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|_2\le\delta$.

Assume a uniform local quadratic likelihood expansion: for $h\in C_n$,

$$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^TZ_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+r_n(h),$$

where $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$ and, for every $R>0$, $\sup\{|r_n(h)|:h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R\}\to_P0$. Assume the full and null local log-likelihoods attain maxima at $\hat h_n\in C_n$ and $\hat h_{0n}\in C_{0n}$ and that both maximizer sequences are tight, meaning that for every $\eta>0$ some $R<\infty$ makes the limiting upper probability of either norm exceeding $R$ at most $\eta$. For

$$T_n:=2\left[\sup_{h\in C_n}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}-\sup_{h\in C_{0n}}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}\right],$$

the likelihood-ratio statistic satisfies

$$T_n\Rightarrow d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C),$$

where $d_I$ is the Fisher-information distance of [[def-fisher-information-metric-distance]]. QMD alone is not asserted to imply the uniform expansion or tightness hypotheses.
Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid real random variables with mean $m$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then $$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nX_k-nm}{\sigma\sqrt n}\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,1).$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Put $q_\mu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$. Direct differentiation gives $q'_\mu=(x-\mu)q_\mu/(2\sigma^2)$ and $q''_\mu=((x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^4)-1/(2\sigma^2))q_\mu$. Its square is a polynomial times $p_\mu=q_\mu^2$. By [F8] and [F9], $\int (x-\mu)^2p_\mu\,dx=\sigma^2$ and $\int (x-\mu)^4p_\mu\,dx=3\sigma^4$, so $\|q''_\mu\|_2^2=3/(16\sigma^4)<\infty$. Also $s_\mu=2q'_\mu/q_\mu=(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$ has second moment $1/\sigma^2$. The identity $q''_a(x)=q''_0(x-a)$ and [F12] give the same norm for every real shift $a$. With $\sigma=1$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F13] gives $E|X-\mu|\le1$, so the even normal density [F1] gives $E(X-\mu)=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$. The two-variable functions $(x,v)\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $(x,u)\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous. To verify the needed product measurability locally, the rectangles $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational endpoints form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$: inside any open ball about a point, density of the rationals gives a rational rectangle containing that point and contained in the ball. Every open subset is therefore the union of the subfamily of these rectangles contained in it, hence a countable union of measurable product rectangles. Thus preimages of open subsets under these continuous functions belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and also to the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. Their squares and restrictions to compact parameter intervals are consequently product measurable, as required by Tonelli below.

For fixed $x$, the functions $v\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $u\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous on each compact interval. By [F10] they are Riemann integrable, by [F15] their integrals are respectively $q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ and $q_{\mu+t}(x)-q_\mu(x)-tq'_\mu(x)$, and [F11] identifies these with their Lebesgue integrals under the assumed AC. Reversed endpoints give the same identities for negative $u,t$.

Cauchy–Schwarz [F13] on the interval between $0$ and $u$, then Tonelli [F14] and step 1.1, gives $\|q'_{\mu+u}-q'_\mu\|_2^2\le u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2$. The second identity of step 2.1 and another Cauchy–Schwarz/Tonelli application give $\|q_{\mu+t}-q_\mu-tq'_\mu\|_2^2\le |t|\int_0^{|t|}u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2du=|t|^4\|q''_0\|_2^2/3=o(t^2)$. For negative $t$ use $q'_{\mu-u}$ on the length-$|t|$ interval; the same first bound holds. This proves QMD with the explicitly supplied normal densities, score $s_\mu$, and positive information $1/\sigma^2$ by [F7].

Under $\mu=0$, the local sets are $C_n=\mathbb R$ and $C_{0n}=(-\infty,0]$ for every $n$, so they are already their limiting closed convex cones. Direct expansion gives $\ell_n(h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(0)=hZ_n-h^2/2$ with $Z_n=\sqrt n\bar X_n$ and zero remainder. The full and null local maximizers are $Z_n$ and $\min(0,Z_n)$. By [F4] and the mean and variance from step 1.1, $Z_n\Rightarrow G\sim N(0,1)$. Choose a large $R$ with $P(|G|\ge R)$ small and apply [F5] to the closed tails to see that both maximizer sequences are tight. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $I=1$.

Completing the square in $\ell_n(\mu)$ gives the full MLE $\bar X_n$ and the constrained MLE $\min(0,\bar X_n)$. Hence the finite-sample likelihood-ratio statistic is $T_n=2[\ell_n(\bar X_n)-\ell_n(\min(0,\bar X_n))]=n(\bar X_n\vee0)^2=(Z_n\vee0)^2$. By [F5], $T_n\Rightarrow(G\vee0)^2$. Its CDF is $0$ for $t<0$ and $P(G\le\sqrt t)=\Phi(\sqrt t)$ for $t\ge0$, so it has mass $1/2$ at zero. By symmetry, $P(G^2\le t)=2\Phi(\sqrt t)-1$ for $t\ge0$, while [F1] gives $P(G=0)=0$; hence $(G\vee0)^2$ has the mixture law $\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\mathcal L(G^2)=\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not $\chi_1^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from a probability law $P$ that is misspecified relative to the density family $p_\theta$, and let $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ be as in [[def-pseudo-true-parameter-under-misspecification]]. Write $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $M(\theta)=\mathbb E_P\ell_\theta(X)$. Assume that $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and that $\theta^*$ is the unique separated interior maximizer of $M$, where interior means that some Euclidean open ball about $\theta^*$ lies in $\Theta$: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\eta_\varepsilon>0$ such that $M(\theta^*)-M(\theta)\ge\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$, so $X\overset{d}=\tau Z$. Direct integration gives $E|Z|=2(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty z e^{-z^2/2}dz=\sqrt{2/\pi}<\infty$, so symmetry gives $E Z=0$. Since $\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z)$ and $z^k\phi(z)\to0$ at both tails, integration by parts gives $E Z^2=\int z^2\phi(z)dz=1$ and $E Z^4=\int z^4\phi(z)dz=3\int z^2\phi(z)dz=3$. Hence $E_PX=0$, $E_PX^2=\tau^2$, and $E_PX^4=3\tau^4$. The fitted log-density is $\ell_\theta(x)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12(x-\theta)^2$. The functions $1$, $X$, and $X^2$ are integrable by the finite absolute first and second moments just established. Thus the expanded log-density is a finite linear combination of integrable functions, and [F9] gives $E_P(X-\theta)^2=E_PX^2-2\theta E_PX+\theta^2$. Therefore $M(\theta)=E_P\ell_\theta(X)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12(\tau^2+\theta^2)$, so $\theta^*=0$ is the unique separated maximizer, and $H=E_P\partial_\theta S_{\theta^*}(X)=-1$.

The uniform criterion error is bounded by $\sup_{\theta\in[-1,1]}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\le\tfrac12|P_nX^2-\tau^2|+|P_nX|$. Put $Y_i=X_i$ and $W_i=X_i^2-\tau^2$. All terms of the following single-variable expansions are integrable by the finite first, second, and fourth moments in step 1.1. Linearity [F9] therefore gives $\mathbb E_PY_i=\mathbb E_PW_i=0$, $\mathbb E_PY_i^2=\tau^2$, and $\mathbb E_PW_i^2=3\tau^4-2\tau^2\mathbb E_PX_i^2+\tau^4=2\tau^4$. Moreover $\mathbb E_P|Y_i|=\tau\mathbb E|Z|<\infty$ and $\mathbb E_P|W_i|\le\mathbb E_PX_i^2+\tau^2=2\tau^2$, so [F8] applies to these variables. By independence and [F8], all cross expectations $\mathbb E_P[Y_iY_j]$ and $\mathbb E_P[W_iW_j]$ vanish for $i\ne j$. For either centered family $V_i=Y_i$ or $V_i=W_i$, $|V_iV_j|\le(V_i^2+V_j^2)/2$ makes every mixed product integrable. Thus [F9] permits termwise expectation of each finite square expansion and gives $\mathbb E_P[(P_nX)^2]=\tau^2/n$ and $\mathbb E_P[(P_nX^2-\tau^2)^2]=2\tau^4/n$. Applying [F5] to these squared deviations gives $P_nX\to_P0$ and $P_nX^2\to_P\tau^2$ by [F7], proving the required uniform law.

The exact constrained MLE is $\hat\theta_n=\Pi_{[-1,1]}(\bar X_n)$, the projection of the sample mean onto $[-1,1]$. step 2.1 and [F7] give $\bar X_n\to_P0$, hence $\hat\theta_n\to_P0$ and the separated-criterion consistency condition holds. On $\{|\bar X_n|\le1\}$ the score equation is exact: $P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=\bar X_n-\hat\theta_n=0$. The complementary event has probability tending to zero, so $\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$. The score is $S_\theta(x)=x-\theta$, its second moment at $\theta^*=0$ under $P$ is $J=\tau^2$, and the sample Hessian is identically $-1$, so the Hessian law holds with $H=-1$.

All hypotheses of [F4] now hold. It gives $\sqrt n\hat\theta_n\Rightarrow N(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T})=N(0,\tau^2)$. The fitted model's score second moment at $\theta=0$ is $E_{N(0,1)}[(X-0)^2]=1$, so the sandwich variance $\tau^2$ differs from the inverse fitted-model information $1$ because $\tau^2\ne1$.
